tagline: A river, a song and the villages along the Blanchard
intro: The Old Mill Stream Scenic Byway follows the Blanchard River on US 224 and State Route 37 in Putnam and Hancock counties. The river drains a rural farming region. Ohio's Department of Transportation presents the scenic byway as a connection among small villages, parks, landmarks and Findlay, with a name inspired by the song “Down by the Old Mill Stream.”

Tell Taylor wrote the song on the Blanchard's banks in Findlay in 1908. Publication followed in 1910, when the vaudeville quartet The Orpheus Comedy Four introduced it to audiences. A Kansas City performance sold all 1,000 copies of sheet music Taylor had brought to a Woolworth store. Sales eventually exceeded four million copies, and the song became a barbershop-quartet staple.

Begin with Glandorf, northwest of Ottawa, then continue to Gilboa's fiberglass bull at US 224 and Pearl Street, followed by Findlay and its courthouse. The river flows west through Findlay and past Ottawa, so this west-to-east journey runs upstream. State Route 37 is the byway's other highway through the Blanchard River region.

moments.title: St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, Glandorf
moments.text: A 169-foot spire rises from Glandorf's Neo-Gothic church, a successor to the small log cabin that served the first congregation. Father Johann Wilhelm Horstmann and other settlers arrived from Glandorf, Germany, in 1834. Their first church also served as his home. The present building was dedicated in 1878. A 1992 fire damaged its interior; during a later restoration in 2017, workers removed a lowered vestibule ceiling to uncover a stained-glass window. The 2017 work also added storm windows to protect the church’s stained glass. Beside the church, Pioneer cemetery holds Horstmann's grave.
moments.notice: The Neo-Gothic church has a 169-foot spire.

moments.title: Gilboa
moments.text: Gilboa's 16-foot fiberglass bull arrived with a transport problem. The installation came as Gilboa sought to draw visitors into its shops and restaurants. Peter Diller placed it at US 224 and Pearl Street in the 1970s, after his father bought it from a bar in Toledo. Diller recalled that its height made stoplights difficult to negotiate and that the bull struck the first one on its forehead. He said the town wanted something representing the community's strength. The statue became a landmark for travelers passing through Gilboa on US 224.
moments.notice: The fiberglass bull stands 16 feet tall at US 224 and Pearl Street.

moments.title: Hancock County Courthouse
moments.text: Findlay's courthouse grew more elaborate as oil and natural gas were discovered in Hancock County. Planned in 1885 to replace a brick courthouse, the new building went up between 1886 and 1888. A copper John Hancock stands atop the clock tower, with three copper figures below him representing Law, Justice and Mercy. A storm blew Hancock off the building in 1922; the statue was repaired the next year. The tower's four clock faces point in the four cardinal directions. Their hand-wound mechanism was electrified in 1925. Inside, original brass railings and medallions survived the courthouse’s extensive restoration during the 1990s.
